Standard 5-minute ONC spectrograms from the network. More clips on [SoundCloud](https://soundcloud.com/oceannetworkscanada) and [Voices in the Sea](https://voicesinthesea.ucsd.edu/index.html).

::: {.dp-panel}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Expand to learn how to read a spectrogram

ONC spectrograms (Hydrophone Viewer and the `.png` / `.pdf` HSD product) are usually **5-minute** files. They use the same axes every time:

* **x-axis**: time
* **y-axis**: frequency (Hz)
* **colour**: sound level in $\text{dB re } 1~\mu\mathrm{Pa}^2/\mathrm{Hz}$

How to read features on the plot:

* A **thin horizontal line** is a tonal — often a nearby instrument, a propeller, or electrical noise.
* A **vertical smear** or filled band is broadband — ships, earthquakes, weather, or a passing animal.
* A **flat-topped** burst or hard colour ceiling is often clipping or saturation.
* **Holes or fading** can be multipath or a quiet moment, not automatically a failed hydrophone.

If the filename includes **LPF** or **HPF**, the band is incomplete after naval screening. See [Data Diversion](13-data-diversion.qmd).
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
::: {.sound-card}
::: {.sound-card-visual}
![Spectrogram of snowmobile noise at Cambridge Bay.](../images/snowmobile.png){lightbox=true group="sound-gallery"}
:::
::: {.sound-card-body}
<p class="sound-card-title">Snowmobile</p>
<p class="sound-card-caption">Cambridge Bay, NU</p>
::: {.sound-card-note}
The soundscape is dominated by surface-coupled noise. In winter, snowmobiles create distinct harmonic bands ($10^2$ to $10^3$ Hz). These overlap with ringed seal vocalizations, creating a high risk of **acoustic masking** in shallow ice-covered leads.

[Marine soundscapes of the Arctic and human impacts: going beyond the "shipping bands"](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44384-025-00038-1)
:::
```{=html}
<audio class="listen-audio" controls preload="metadata"></audio>
```
